In this example, the card read 'Supportive for gold'. Large speculators were net long +171.4k, with 212.6k longs against 41.2k shorts. That sat at the 35th percentile of the year: a few fewer longs than usual, not washed out, so only slight support.

The slider puts it on one line, from few longs and supportive to crowded and a headwind. The same card also read the yen: speculators crowded long, so less haven fuel left for a risk-off move.

COT positioning sits on the Drivers tab and covers large speculators, commercials and small traders. Context for your own entry method, not signals.

05.hook: One loud day shouldn't rename the market.
05.ig_caption:
One loud day shouldn't rename the market.

That's the rule behind the regime sheet in MarketDynamics 2.0. A challenger has to lead on 2 readings in a row before the regime's name changes.

In the example shown, deflationary risk-off was the confirmed regime at 19%, gold's best backdrop. Liquidation had overtaken it at 46%, but it was only on day 1 of 2 to confirm. So the label held.

Why build it that way? Cross-asset markets are noisy. A single session of dollar strength or a wobble in bonds can tilt the odds for a day and reverse the next. A regime call that flip-flops with every swing tells you nothing useful about how to approach gold.

What you get on the Drivers tab: the confirmed regime, the challenger and how close it is to confirming, and a plain-English line on what a shift would mean for gold. Context for your own plan, not signals.
